rv.q: Aside from a few clanging scenes, it’s a gorgeously executed celebration of a pained subject’s artistry.

That’s a transition, not since equaled, that director-choreographer Christopher Wheeldon, book write Lynn Nottage and an impeccable cast led by the star-is-born Myles Frost, bring to pulse-quickening life on the stage.
MJ, a remarkable Broadway musical written by Lynn Nottage and directed and choreographed by Christopher Wheeldon, deftly probes this weighty topic.
The show is a slick, professionally mounted tribute that will satisfy Jackson's devoted fans, but it doesn't dig deep enough to reveal the complex humanity of its subject.

Even the combined power of Jackson’s material and Wheeldon’s reanimation of it cannot make up for the emptiness at its center; we cannot understand or accept the main character if he’s deliberately kept from us.
That’s just one very large disingenuous note in an altogether baffling production that opened Tuesday at the Theatre.

It’s also a discomfiting experience, in both what’s obviously left off-stage (this is a commercial Broadway musical which ejected a Variety reporter for asking cast about the allegations at the premiere) and its portrayal of Michael Jackson as a lonely Peter Pan in turmoil.

"The dancers and singers of the ensemble, who double as secondary characters, are first-rate, and Wheeldon gives them a lot to do. Most of the songs are performed as rehearsals or flashbacks, which is to say as full-on production numbers. (Tracks from Jackson’s 1995 album HIStory are cannily placed by Nottage as character moments.

And yet — you knew that was coming, didn’t you? — for all its surface flash and stylish presentation, “MJ” comes across, like most jukebox/bio-musical hybrids, as superficial fan-bait: a glossy but unrevelatory moonwalk through the ups and downs (mostly the ups) of Jackson’s career.
The sequence is novel, invigorating and smart — exactly what the rest of “MJ” isn’t.
Only the music and movement in MJ work — the show’s Michael, Myles Frost, glides and hip-rocks through a physical impersonation that operates above and beyond the show’s own ugly logic.
If audience reaction is any indication MJ is a hit worthy of The King of Pop’s impeccable standards.
And the barrage of heavily rhythmic songs, accompanied by the onslaught of Jackson-style movement, tends to blend together and teeter on tiresomeness.
MJ is the platinum standard the often uninspired, generic jukebox musical could benefit to emulate.
MJ comes as close as any musical that has appeared on a Broadway stage in a very long time.
They won't be disappointed by MJ.
It’s an evening of extraordinary performances and stunning choreography, as much a live concert of Michael Jackson’s greatest hits as a biographical or jukebox musical.
There are thrills and there are chills.
For everything else, MJ The Musical is a thriller.

"MJ The Musical," which recently opened at the Neil Simon Theatre in New York City Tuesday, features tracks from "Off the Wall," "Thriller," "Bad," "Dangerous" — and classics from The Jackson 5. Like most jukebox musicals, there are good scenes.
It also (much like Michael Jackson himself) comes at a price, and one that the producers weren’t willing to acknowledge, perhaps out of fear of hurting their own commercial success.

And if there's one thing audiences love, it's a show with good songs. "MJ The Musical," which recently opened at the Neil Simon Theatre, features tracks from "Off the Wall," "Thriller," "Bad," "Dangerous" — and classics from The Jackson 5. Like most jukebox musicals, there are good scenes.
MJ is a strange experience, at once dazzling and unsatisfying, a peerless display of pizzazz with nothing underneath.
You'll leave the Theatre (where the show opens tonight) both on a giddy high from Jackson's music but also grappling with what was and wasn't incorporated.
It’s a credit to everyone involved in MJ, then, that there’s no shortage of joy here.
MJ is both wonderfully fun and predictably blinkered.
Taken as an entertainment MJ satisfies immensely, but as drama not so much.
But as Jackson says in the second act, “We have the icing, but it doesn’t mean anything unless the cake tastes good,” and no amount of frosting could make this amoral mud pie any easier to swallow.
This is a slickly corporate, officially sanctioned slice of legacy clean-up.
And that is only one of the minor offenses on display in “MJ,” which opened Tuesday at Broadway’s Theatre.
This is a star-making tour de force performance requiring a level of singing, dancing and nuanced acting rarely seen on stage.
Perhaps that is what the estate actually wanted; to rejuvenate its coffers by sending audiences thirsting for the real thing.
His mimicry of Jackson’s dance steps, speaking voice, singing voice, mannerisms and attitude made his not exact resemblance utterly irrelevant.

cn.t: Dazzling choreography and electrifying musical numbers thrill, but critics find this estate-approved biomusical a slick, sanitized tribute that sidesteps controversy and offers little depth beyond spectacular dancing and Jackson's iconic hits.

sg.ra: For MJ the Musical's dance-heavy choreography, Center Orchestra rows A-H sit entirely in front of the mezzanine overhang (which begins at row J) and deliver head-on sightlines of the performers' feet — critical for a Michael Jackson dance biomusical. Row A seats 107-110 are frequently cited as the theatre's best, but rows C-D balance proximity with neck-angle comfort.

Because Neil Simon's orchestra is unusually deep (25 rows, A-Z) and the mezzanine overhang only starts cutting the top of the stage noticeably by row S, rows H-P give you full head-on views with no overhang effect at non-premium pricing — a specific quirk of this house's long orchestra footprint.

The mezzanine overhang is felt from row J onward and by rows S-Z it actively cuts off the top of the stage per SeatPlan's orchestra guide — a real issue for MJ the Musical, which uses tall set pieces and lifts. Unique to Neil Simon because the orchestra runs all the way to row Z, pushing rear seats deep under the overhang.

Front Center Mezzanine rows A-B give an elevated, unobstructed sweep — particularly valuable at Neil Simon because MJ the Musical uses formation choreography that reads better from above. Tripadvisor users confirm no obstruction issues at front mezz (photo cited from row A seat 103). Row A also has the best legroom in the mezzanine.

Specific Neil Simon quirk: Left and Right Mezzanine rows H and L sit directly behind railings that border the internal staircase, making legroom 'very tight' — SeatPlan calls out seats H1-7 and L9-15 by number. This is a house-specific hazard, not the generic 'Broadway legroom is tight' complaint.

Rear mezzanine at Neil Simon has a shallow rake — a specific architectural quirk noted by SeatPlan — so rows S-U feel distant and lose detail on the stage front, and the mezzanine's own underside can minor-obstruct the back-row view. For MJ's facial-expression moments in 'Man in the Mirror' numbers this is a real detriment.

Three boxes are staggered off the Left Mezzanine at Neil Simon — a specific architectural feature of this house — and SeatPlan explicitly states the viewing experience 'isn't the best' because the angle is fully side-on. Priced as premium but not worth it for a dance musical where frontal sightlines matter.
